title: Vow Text for Founding the Pure Land Society During a Serious Illness
author: by Master Ouyi
excerpt: On the thirteenth day of the twelfth month of the jiawu year. I, Zhixu, a disciple under the bodhisattva precepts, with one mind take refuge in Amitābha Buddha of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, in Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, the pure ocean-wide assembly, and in all the Three Jewels of the ten directions and the three periods.

inline.s: “On the thirteenth day of the twelfth month of the jiawu year. I, Zhixu, a disciple under the bodhisattva precepts, with one mind take refuge in Amitābha Buddha of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, in Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, the pure ocean-wide assembly, and in all the Three Jewels of the ten directions and the three periods.”
on the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, I, Zhixu, a disciple under the bodhisattva precepts, with one mind take refuge in Amitābha Buddha of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, and in Avalokiteśvara
, and in all the Three Jewels of the ten directions and the three periods.

[The thirteenth day of the twelfth month of the jiawu year] That is, the 13th day of the 12th lunar month of 1654 CE. This text was written a little over a month before Master Ouyi passed away; the Master died on the 21st day of the 1st lunar month of the following year (yiwei, 1655
Master Ouyi’s lay surname was Zhong, his given name Jiming, and his courtesy name Ouyi.
At twenty-three he resolved to leave home and investigate the great matter.

At twenty-four he dreamed of Master Hanshan three times in one month; Hanshan was then living at Caoxi, too far to travel, so he took the tonsure under Hanshan’s disciple Xueling and was given the name Zhixu.

Painfully I reflect that I, Zhixu, left home at twenty-four for the great matter of birth and death, without the slightest wish to set myself up as a teacher. Unexpectedly, pressed by illusory conditions, I wrongly became a teacher. For more than twenty years, though I had the slight merit of spreading the Dharma, I was burdened by empty fame; my contemplative practice grew lax, and I could not subdue the afflictions to ascend to the five grades.
the great matter of birth and death, left home at twenty-four, absolutely
the slightest wish to set myself up as a teacher. Un
illusory conditions, I wrongly became a teacher. For more than twenty years
and my actual practice (contemplative practice) grew lax
to ascend to the five grades of contemplative practice.

[Contemplative practice] To contemplate the principle in the mind and practice in the body according to the principle. [Lax] The same as “neglected,” becoming rusty through lack of practice. [Five grades] That is, the “five grades of contemplative practice,” which is the contemplative-practice stage of Buddhahood among the six stages of identity with Buddhahood; this stage accomplishes the merit of the five grades, hence it is called “the five grades of contemplative practice.” The five grades are: 1. the grade of sympathetic joy
3. the grade of expounding the Dharma
4. the grade of practicing the six perfections in part

5. the grade of correctly practicing the six perfections. [Six stages of identity with Buddhahood] The six stages marking the progression from ordinary being to Buddhahood: 1. Buddhahood in principle — all sentient beings, though transmigrating through the six paths and dwelling day by day amid worldly toil and affliction, turned away from the body of enlightenment, are nonetheless fully endowed with the merit of the Buddha-nature; hence it is called “Buddhahood in principle.” 2. Buddhahood in name — one hears, either from a good spiritual friend or from the scriptures, that the mind is inherently endowed with the unborn and unceasing Buddha-nature, and comprehends and understands it in name, with a sudden awakening; hence it is called “Buddhahood in name.” 3. Buddhahood in contemplative practice — not only understanding the name, but further cultivating contemplation according to the teachings, so that the mind’s contemplation is clear and principle and wisdom correspond; hence it is called “Buddhahood in contemplative practice.” (Principle and wisdom corresponding means: principle is the contemplated realm of principle, and wisdom is the contemplating wisdom; correspondence means equivalence, that is, realm and wisdom are well matched, and words and deeds are consistent.) 4. Buddhahood in resemblance — the practitioner at this stage, in contemplative practice, contemplates more and more clearly and stills more and more deeply; though not yet truly awakened and realized, he is, in principle, nearly the same as one who has truly realized; hence it is called “Buddhahood in resemblance.” 5. Buddhahood in partial realization — this is, after the ten stages of faith, to break through one portion of ignorance and realize one portion of the three virtues, thereby entering the first abode and realizing the dharmakāya, becoming a great being of the dharmakāya. From then on, from the first abode upward, each stage breaks through ignorance and realizes the three virtues, until equal enlightenment, altogether passing through forty-one stages and breaking through forty-one portions; hence it is called “Buddhahood in partial realization.” 6. Buddhahood in ultimate realization — from equal enlightenment, breaking through the last portion of ignorance, delusion is exhausted and truth is pure, and one fully realizes the tathatā Buddha-nature inherent in the present body, entering the stage of wonderful enlightenment and attaining Buddhahood; hence it is called “Buddhahood in ultimate realization.”

Now, afflicted by illness, though my mind is clear, my strength is not my own; I weep and cry out, not knowing what to do. Fortunately, relying on the Buddha’s compassion, my last breath has not yet ceased. If I do not urgently press on in the pure karma, how shall I ever escape the wheel of suffering?
that illness besets my body, and my heart
clearly understands that right mindfulness should be raised and maintained,
my strength is not my own; I weep and cry out,
has not yet ended (if it ended at this moment, the consequences would be unthinkable); if I do not urgently press on in the pure karma
how shall I ever escape the wheel of birth and death?

[Cry out (haohu)] To wail and weep aloud. [Right mindfulness] The right mindfulness of the Pure Land school is the thought of reciting the Buddha’s name without admixture of delusive thoughts (thought following thought in succession); the right mindfulness of the Chan school is no-thought (the non-arising of a single thought). [Not knowing what to do] At a loss what to do. Wang means “not”; you means “that which.” [Press on (xù)] To strive with effort. [Wheel of suffering] The bitter fruit of birth and death revolves without ceasing, hence it is called a

The Chan school has a similar public case: Chan Master Keqin (the teacher of Master Dahui, and the leader of the Chan school between the Northern and Southern Song), in his youth, was widely versed in the scriptures and teachings, and took refuge under Wuzu Fayan (Chan Master Fayan of Mount Wuzu). One day he entered the master’s room to seek instruction, and Keqin reported the state of his cultivation and realization, asking Wuzu for confirmation. However he phrased it, Wuzu said it still would not do. Keqin was unconvinced, and, relying on his wide learning in the scriptures and his eloquence, began to argue boldly with Wuzu. Wuzu, greatly displeased, said:
can this routine of yours end birth and death
When the day comes that you sit alone under the solitary lamp in the nirvāṇa hall, test it for yourself
(at the time of death, verify it yourself)
Keqin left in anger. When he reached Jinshan, he fell gravely ill.
In his peril and distress, he applied all that he had learned in his life
(at this moment of peril, to raise right mindfulness and maintain it (no-thought) by means of all that he had learned in his life)
and not a single thing was of any use
in ordinary days he only sought to talk glibly, but at the end of life it was utterly useless!
Recalling Wuzu’s words, he then vowed:
“As soon as my illness eases a little
(as soon as my illness improves even slightly)

Later, when he had recovered somewhat, he packed his bundle and returned. Wuzu was delighted at the sight of him (knowing he was material worth shaping), made him his attendant, and Keqin eventually inherited the robe and bowl (at last he inherited Wuzu’s robe and bowl).
[Nirvāṇa hall] The place where sick monks are sent to enter extinction.
This public case warns us: empty talk — armchair strategizing — is the great taboo of a Buddhist practitioner!
[Armchair strategizing] Sitting and talking, debating at length with a torrent of words, yet when facing the battle and the enemy, utterly without ability.

Therefore I rouse a sincere heart and, reverently, in the scripture hall of Lingfeng, invite ten fellow practitioners of the same aspiration and five lay-protector bodhisattva novices to join, with minds in harmony, in forming a society for three years. Each day, in three periods we recite the liturgy and laud and bow before the great name, and in two periods we sit in stillness. We will study the great canon exhaustively, cultivating both doctrine and contemplation, and holding both the precepts and the teachings as urgent. I vow that, together with all beings of the Dharma realm, we shall surely be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

Therefore. [Scripture hall] The scripture hall, the building where the canon is stored. [Three periods a day] In ancient times twelve periods made up one day and night, one period being equal to two of today’s hours. [Still meditation] To sit in stillness with single-minded concentration.
[Great canon] An abbreviation of the Great Canon of scriptures. [Doctrine and contemplation] The study of doctrine and contemplative
. [Precepts and teachings] Jie means the precepts; cheng means the teachings. [Urgent (ji)]

From now on, I, Zhixu, vow not to ascend the seat and preach the Dharma, except that I dare not weary of answering my fellow practitioners who hold the scriptures and ask about their meaning. As for expounding the texts and unfolding their meaning, there are Zhaonan, Lingsheng, and Xingdan, who can proclaim them somewhat. I vow not to sit level with my back to the Buddha, except to sit slightly turned or facing an image. I vow not to ascend the platform to confer the precepts; for conferring precepts and studying the Vinaya there are Zhaonan and Dengci who can instruct. I vow not to accept invitations to meals from lay people, except within the quiet rooms of a monastery.

I look up and beg the Three Jewels to bear witness and receive me, so that, if my conditions are not yet exhausted, I may soon attain ease and peace; and if my final limit cannot be escaped, I may go straight back to the Land of Peace and Nourishment. In life, I shall recite the Buddha’s name and write as well; in death, I shall neither fall nor regress.

[Land of Peace and Nourishment] Another name for the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.

I further vow that my fellow practitioners, whether I, Zhixu, live or not, will hold firm their resolve and cultivate together, with a beginning and an end. I further vow that the lay-protector novices, whether I live or not, will manage affairs with a sincere heart, without slackness or error. With this supreme and excellent pure cause, I dedicate the merit toward the unsurpassed ultimate fruit, so that, together with all sentient beings, we may all return to the secret store.

[Ultimate fruit] The ultimate stage of fruition, that is, the fruit of Buddhahood. [Sentient beings] Creatures that possess life. [All] Wholly, entirely. [Secret store] What is hidden and not transmitted to people is called “secret”; what is stored up within is called “store.” The “secret store” refers to the wondrous Dharma of all Buddhas, which the Buddhas guard well and do not proclaim recklessly.

Chan Master Yuanwu Keqin Foguo, of the lay surname Luo, was a native of Pengzhou (in present-day Sichuan), whose ancestors had been Confucian scholars for generations. As a child his memory was superb, and he could commit a thousand words to memory each day.

In his youth, Chan Master Keqin traveled to various places to study, and finally took refuge under Wuzu Fayan (Chan Master Fayan of Mount Wuzu). Under Wuzu’s strict and pressing guidance (zā), after many twists and turns, he finally attained great awakening and received the robe and bowl.

His greatest contribution to the history of Chinese Chan was to push Chinese Chan culture to its brilliant summit with two works, the Blue Cliff Record and the Essentials of Yuanwu’s Mind. The Blue Cliff Record in particular was called at the time “the foremost book of the Chan school.”

During the Chongning era of the Northern Song, Keqin returned to Shu to visit his aged mother; Guo Zhizhang, the military governor of Chengdu, invited him to preside over Zhaojue Monastery (in Chengdu), where he stayed for eight years, expounding the sudden teaching on a grand scale and raising aloft the school’s style, so that monks from all over the country flocked to Shu to study. From then on, Zhaojue Monastery entered the most flourishing period of its history, and in one stroke established its lofty position as the ancestral seat of the Linji school of Chan, winning the reputation of “the foremost Chan grove west of Sichuan.” After Chan Master Keqin took up residence at Zhaojue Monastery, Emperor Gaozong of the Song by imperial decree renamed Zhaojue Monastery a “Chan grove,” making it the greatest Chan cave in Shu. It produced eminent monks in abundance, the most of all Shu.

At the height of his fame, Chan Master Keqin, at the invitation of the chancellor Li Gang, presided over the Dharma at Jinshan Monastery in Zhenjiang, known as “the crown of the Chan groves south of the Yangtze.” In this famous grove that produced eminent monks in abundance, Chan Master Keqin displayed the Linji style to the full, with staff and shout flying in turn and the sharp point flashing like lightning; in a single evening he brought seventeen of the assembly’s students to awakening, and his fame resounded through the Chan groves of the world, so that his meditation hall was named “Great Awakening.”

As early as the end of the Northern Song, when Chan Master Keqin was residing at Jiangshan Monastery in Jinling, the Dharma flourished so greatly that there was scarcely room for all who sought to study under him. At that time Emperor Huizong of the Song treated him with courtesy and bestowed upon him a purple kāṣāya and the title “Foguo” (Buddha Fruit). Later, when Emperor Gaozong of the Southern Song visited Yangzhou, he likewise summoned Chan Master Keqin, then abbot of Jinshan Monastery in Zhenjiang, to ask about the Way, greatly admired his practice and wisdom, treated him with the rites due a national teacher, and bestowed the title “Yuanwu” (Perfect Awakening).

In the fifth year of the Shaoxing era of the Southern Song (1135), on the fifth day of the eighth month, he manifested his passing. As the end approached, an attendant brought paper and brush and asked for a verse. He wrote: “Already fully realized, with no merit to display, there is no need to leave a verse; I merely show this to accord with conditions — take care, take care.” He cast aside the brush and passed away, at the age of seventy-three.
